﴿By the Clear Book﴾ It is mentioned in az-Zukhruf (43:2). It is an oath (qasam), and its answer is ﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾. It was also said that its answer is ﴿Indeed, We were ever warning﴾, but this is far-fetched.

﴿Indeed, We sent it down on a blessed night﴾. He means the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr) in Ramadan. As for how it was sent down: it was sent down to the lowest heaven all at once, and then Jibril brought it down upon the Prophet ﷺ piece by piece. It was also said that the meaning is that its revelation began on the Night of Decree. It was also said that the blessed night is the night of the middle of Sha'ban, but this is false, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ (al-Qadr: 1), together with His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan is that in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ (al-Baqarah: 185).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verse 4:

﴿In it every wise affair is made distinct.﴾ The meaning of "yufraq" (is made distinct) is "yufassal" (is detailed) and "yukhallas" (is separated out). The "wise affair" (amr hakim) is the provision and the lifespans of the servants, and all their affairs in that year, copied from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) on the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr), so that the angels may act upon that throughout the following year. It has been said that this takes place on the night of the middle of Sha'ban, but this is false, for what we have already mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verse 5:

﴿Amran min ʿindinā﴾ is an object (maf'ul) of a suppressed verb, in the sense of specification (ikhtisas), as said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAtiyya said it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). It was also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). ﴿Mursilīn﴾: the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them. It was also said: it refers to the sending of mercy. The first is more evident.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verse 10:

﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke.﴾ On this there are two opinions. The first is the view of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Ibn ʿAbbas, that the smoke will occur before the Day of Resurrection, afflicting the believer with something like a cold, and making the heads of the disbelievers and hypocrites swell; it is among the portents of the Hour (ashrat al-sa'a). Ḥudhayfa narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first of the portents of the Hour is the smoke."

The second is the view of Ibn Masʿud: that the smoke refers to what befell the Quraysh when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them with drought, so that a man would see smoke between himself and the sky due to the severity of hunger. Ibn Masʿud said: "Five have already passed: the smoke, the seizing (al-lizam), the assault (al-batsha), the moon, and the Byzantines (al-rum)."

﴿This is a painful punishment﴾. It may be that this is the speech of God Most High, or that it is the speech of the people when the smoke overtook them, and this is more apparent, because what follows it is by consensus their speech, so the discourse is coherent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verses 13–14:

﴿Anna lahumu l-dhikra﴾ ("How can they have remembrance?"). This is from the speech of God Most High, and its meaning is a declaration of the improbability of their being reminded, given that they denied the Prophet ﷺ. The "waw" in His saying ﴿wa-qad jaahum﴾ ("while there had already come to them") is the waw of circumstance (waw al-haal). ﴿Rasulun mubin﴾ ("a clear Messenger") means Muhammad ﷺ. ﴿Wa-qaaloo muallamun﴾ ("and they said, 'He is one taught'") means: someone human teaches him.

"A noble messenger" — meaning Musa (peace be upon him): "Deliver to me the servants of Allah." Here "an" is explanatory (mufassirah), standing in place of "say"; "addu" is an imperative verb from al-ada' (to deliver), and "ibad Allah" is its object, referring to the Children of Israel. The meaning is: send the Children of Israel, as He said in Ta-Ha, "Send with us the Children of Israel." It was also said that "ibad Allah" is a vocative (munada), meaning: "Deliver to me obedience and faith, O servants of Allah." The first view is more apparent.

"And do not exalt yourselves against Allah" — i.e., do not be arrogant — "with an authority" — i.e., with proof and clear evidence. "Indeed, I seek refuge in my Lord and your Lord from your stoning me" — it is disputed whether this means stoning with stones or reviling; the first view is more apparent. "So leave me alone" — i.e., keep away from me and let me go my way.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verse 23–27:

﴿So travel by night with My servants﴾. This is a command from God to Musa, peace be upon him, and "the servants" here refers to the Children of Israel; that is, take them out by night. ﴿Indeed, you will be pursued﴾. This is an informing that Fir'awn and his hosts will pursue them. ﴿And leave the sea [as it is], motionless﴾. That is, still in its state. It was also said: dry. It is narrated that when Musa crossed the sea, he wanted to strike it with his staff so that it would close up as it had when he struck it and it split. God said to him: Leave it as it is, so that Fir'awn and his people will enter it and drown in it. It was also said: the meaning of rahwan is smooth, and it was said: open and wide. ﴿And springs﴾. It may be that this refers to the channels branching out from the Nile, and there were springs at that time. It was also said that it means gold and silver, but this is far-fetched. ﴿And a noble station﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions: the pulpits and the fine dwellings. ﴿And luxury﴾, from enjoying provisions and other things. ﴿In which they took delight﴾. That is, they were enjoying themselves. It was also said: rejoicing, and it was said: possessors of fruit.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verse 28:

﴿Thus﴾ is in the accusative position, meaning: like that expulsion, We expelled them; or it is in the nominative position, its sense being: the matter is thus. ﴿And We caused other people to inherit it﴾. He means the Children of Israel. This is related by al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhshari) and al-Mawardi (al-Mawardi), but Ibn Attiyya (Ibn ʿAtiyya) weakened it, saying: "Because it is not narrated in the well-known histories that the Children of Israel returned to Egypt at that time." Al-Hasan (al-Hasan) said that they did return to it. What indicates that the intended people are the Children of Israel is His saying in Surah al-Shu'ara: ﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 59].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verse 29:

﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them﴾ In this there are three opinions. The first is that it is an expression of their belittlement. When a distinguished man died, the Arabs would say in glorifying him: "The heaven and the earth wept for him," using it as a figure of speech and hyperbole. The meaning, then, is that these people are not such, because they are too insignificant to be cared about. The second opinion: it has been said that when a believer dies, the place of his worship on earth weeps for him, and the place from which his deeds ascend in the heaven weeps for him. The meaning, then, is that these people are not such, because they are disbelievers, or because they have no righteous deed. The third is that the meaning is: neither the people of the heaven nor the people of the earth wept for them. The first is the more eloquent, and it is a well-known mode of expression in the speech of the Arabs. ﴿They were not given respite﴾, that is, they were not delayed.

﴿We chose them knowingly﴾ means: We knew that they deserved that. ﴿Above the worlds﴾ means: above the people of their time. ﴿A manifest trial﴾ means: a test.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verse 34:

﴿Indeed, these people﴾ means the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿So bring back our forefathers﴾.

Translation:

﴿So bring back our forefathers﴾ — the Quraysh addressed this to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions in a challenging manner (ʿajz, i.e., to show their inability to do so). It is narrated that they asked that Qusayy ibn Kilab be brought back to life for them, so they could ask him about the conditions of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verse 37:

﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾ Tubba' was a king of Himyar, and he was a believer while his people were disbelievers. So he (Allah) censured his people and did not censure him. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not." The meaning of the verse: Are the Quraysh stronger and mightier, or the people of Tubba' and those before them of the disbelievers? We destroyed the people of Tubba' and others when they disbelieved, so likewise We will destroy these. Thus the purpose of the statement is a warning. ﴿And those before them⦗﻿⦘﴾ is in conjunction with "the people of Tubba'." It has also been said that it is a subject (mubtada'), and then one stops at what precedes it, but the first view is more correct.
﴿Playing⁠﻿﻿ (lāʿibīn)﴾ is a negated state (ḥāl manfiyya), mentioned in al-Anbiyāʾ (the chapter of the Prophets).

﴿On a Day when no kinsman (mawla) will avail another kinsman in anything, nor will they be helped, except for those on whom Allah has mercy﴾. Here "mawla" is general, encompassing the close friend (wali), the relative, and the other kinds of kin. ﴿Except for those on whom Allah has mercy﴾ is an exceptive clause that is disconnected (istithna' munqati') if by His words ﴿nor will they be helped﴾ He means the disbelievers, and connected (istithna' muttasil) if by that He means all people.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verses 47–50:

﴿Seize him﴾, i.e., drag him along with harshness. ﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of the boiling water.﴾ What is actually poured is the boiling water (al-hamim), which is hot water; but the poured thing is described here as "the torment" attributed to the boiling water, as a figurative usage (majaz), because that is more eloquent and more awe-inspiring. The original form appears in His saying about ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble!﴾ This is said to the disbeliever in a manner of rebuke and mockery, meaning: you were the mighty and noble in your own estimation. It is narrated that Abu Jahl said: "Between its two mountains (of Makkah) there is no one more mighty or more noble than me." So the verse was revealed. ﴿You used to doubt﴾: a form of ifta'ala from al-muriyah (mirya), which means doubt (shakk).

in a place of security. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "maqam" with a dammah on the meem (مُقام), meaning a place of residence (موضع إقامة), while the rest read it with a fathah (مَقام), meaning a place of standing (موضع قيام). The intended meaning is Paradise. "Amin" is from "al-amn" (security), meaning that one is safe therein (مأمون فيه). It was also said that it is from "al-amnah" (freedom from harm), and the attribute is applied to the place figuratively (مجازاً).

﴿of fine silk and thick brocade﴾: al-sundus is the fine (thin) kind of dibaj (silk brocade), and al-istabraq is the thick kind of it. ﴿Thus﴾ is in the nominative position, meaning the matter is thus, or in the accusative position, meaning "like that We married them." ﴿They call for therein﴾ means they call for their servants. ﴿Except the first death﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same kind as what precedes it). The meaning is that they do not taste death therein, since they had already tasted the first death alone before that. Were it not for His words ﴿therein﴾, it would be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), owing to the generality of the word "death." It has also been said that "illa" here means "after," but this view is weak.

Were it not for His words ﴿therein﴾, it would be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), owing to the generality of the word "death." It has also been said that "illa" here means "after," but this view is weak.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 44, verse 58:

﴿We have made it easy﴾, i.e., We made it simple (sahhalnāhu), with the pronoun referring to the Qur'an; ﴿in your tongue﴾, i.e., in your language, which is the tongue of the Arabs (lisān al-'Arab).

Quran 44:59: ﴿So wait, [O Muhammad], indeed they are waiting﴾. That is: wait for Our victory for you and their destruction, for they are waiting for the opposite of that. So in it is a promise to him and a warning to them.
